html:
Northern Liang was a small state in the Hexi Corridor of northwest China, one of the Sixteen Kingdoms, from 397 to 439, with a remnant in Turpan until 460. The map shows it in 400.

It was ruled by the Juqu family, a non-Chinese clan of the region. Its strongest ruler, Juqu Mengxun, took the oasis cities of the corridor, including Dunhuang, and made Guzang, modern Wuwei, his capital. The corridor was the main road between China and Central Asia, so Northern Liang controlled much of the Silk Road trade.

Its kings were great patrons of Buddhism. The Indian monk Dharmakṣema translated major scriptures in Guzang, and early Buddhist cave shrines were cut in its lands, part of how Buddhism reached China.

In 439 the Northern Wei conquered Guzang and moved many of its people and monks east. The last of the family fled to Gaochang in Turpan, where they ruled until the Rouran destroyed them in 460.
